extracted.intended_audience: PR professionals, corporate communicators, executives, and spokespeople
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how corporate spokespeople and executives should respond to product defects and public backlash, with specific advice on apologies, stakeholder targeting, tone, and delivery. Geared toward preventing and repairing media crises arising from executive comments or flawed products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take responsibility for product flaws
rubrics_metrics.description: Public statements should accept responsibility for flaws in the product rather than deflecting blame.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example corporate statement: “We are committed to making things right so if you purchased product from our store or on our website and you think it is too sheer, we welcome you to return it for a full refund or exchange.” The post praises the March statement as 'tone perfect' and recommends repeating such language during media interviews rather than inventing new explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pledge concrete remediation and customer remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Communications should promise concrete fixes (e.g., work with supplier to replace fabric) and offer clear remedies to affected customers (refunds or exchanges).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state steps being taken to remedy the issue and offer refunds/exchanges as appropriate; this demonstrates commitment to 'making things right' and preserves goodwill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeat the official, tone‑appropriate company statement in interviews
rubrics_metrics.description: When a satisfactory corporate statement has been issued, spokespeople should stick to that statement during subsequent media interviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post notes the company’s March statement was 'tone perfect' and 'should have just been repeated verbatim during any subsequent media interview.' Deviating invites additional damage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not shift blame onto customers
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid implying that product problems are the fault of customers (e.g., body size or user error) as a response to complaints about product quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shifting blame alienates the customer base; even if there's partial factual support, blaming customers is a poor communications strategy and escalates reputational harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid condescension and discriminatory language (e.g., fat‑shaming)
rubrics_metrics.description: Communications must not belittle, stereotype, or shame customers (for example, characterizing some bodies as 'not working' for the product).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post highlights Chip Wilson’s remarks as 'fat‑shaming' and condescending; such remarks are particularly damaging because they attack the people who buy the product and can negate prior good-will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target apologies and messages to affected stakeholders (customers first)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apologies and corrective communications should be directed primarily to the harmed constituency—customers—rather than only to internal audiences like employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An apology directed mainly to employees may satisfy staff but will not repair trust with customers. Employees are an important constituency but should not be addressed to the exclusion of critical stakeholders who keep the company in business.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure apologies convey genuine mea culpa and appropriate tone
rubrics_metrics.description: An effective apology should communicate clear remorse and avoid sounding defensive or merely annoyed at the inconvenience rather than regretful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters noted Wilson's statement 'sounds more like he's annoyed' and 'There is no mea culpa here.' Avoid apologetic statements that read as defensiveness or exasperation—explicitly acknowledge harm and express regret.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delivery matters: maintain eye contact and avoid obviously read/apologetic performance
rubrics_metrics.description: The physical delivery of an apology (eye contact, teleprompter placement, appearing not to be reading) affects perceptions of sincerity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observers noticed Wilson’s eyes 'stray below the screen to what are likely notes' and criticized teleprompter positioning; poor delivery undermines the apology and signals inauthenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceived accountability of executives affects apology credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Apologies by senior executives can be viewed as hollow if leaders are not held to higher standards or do not face consequences similar to lower‑level employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A commenter argues executives often avoid sanctions that others would face for similar mistakes; this double standard makes apologies ring hollow. Communications strategies should account for public expectations of accountability.
